Strong Execution Engine With Room to Evolve. I came to Motion not looking for another productivity app, but for a scheduling layer that could actually think. As someone running multiple business lines simultaneously, I needed something that could bridge strategic planning and daily execution without manual translation every morning. After using Motion as the calendar execution engine inside a larger stack connected to ClickUp for task management, here is what I found. The AI time-blocking is genuinely adaptive. When priorities shift, Motion reschedules intelligently rather than just flagging a conflict. The multi-calendar view across accounts creates coherence where I previously had noise. And the way it works backward from deadlines to build buffer time has real operational value for project-based work. The main friction is the ClickUp integration. Two-way sync requires workarounds and third-party automation to function reliably. For operators who want a clean hands-off pipeline, that gap matters. The mobile experience also lags behind desktop, and the scheduling AI could be more transparent about why it makes the decisions it does. That said, when Motion is positioned correctly in a connected stack, it earns its place as a time intelligence layer. It is not a standalone project management solution, but as the execution engine that translates priorities into a scheduled day, the ROI on reclaimed mental bandwidth is real. Recommended for operators and knowledge workers ready to build around it rather than just drop it in.

Not Enough Support to Justify the Price. Some of Motion’s ideas look brilliant on paper. The promise of automatic scheduling, AI Employees, and a unified command centre for life and work is exactly what someone with multiple projects needs. In reality, you end up spending a lot of time trying to figure out how Motion works on your own. There’s no community space, no group sessions, no Slack or Discord, no live onboarding, no Q&A hours, no human walkthroughs. Nothing that most far-cheaper tools give as standard. You won’t realise this until after you’ve paid. You can message a chatbot, but the conversations are slow, and you only ever receive follow up via email block-by-block. There isn’t a simple way to speak to an actual person and share your screen to solve problems quickly. Because of that, I found myself burning through AI Employee credits just to ask what on earth Motion had done with my task list. After a recent Q4 progress meeting with my business coach, I tried to reflect our discussion inside Motion in a clean, structured way. It was almost impossible. Basic things like dragging and dropping to reorder tasks aren’t supported. You can’t reorder cards inside a kanban column. That goes against every normal project management workflow. It slows you down instead of helping you move. The AI Employees themselves need a lot of manual effort to set up. You can’t simply point them to the SOPs you already have saved in your systems. You have to copy and paste the text from every document into Motion one-by-one to make them usable. That’s a huge amount of double work. I’d get my executive assistant to help with the setup, but adding a second human seat costs 1.5x the price of the first seat. Two seats are more expensive than three. The pricing is aggressive in a way that doesn’t match the level of support you get. The practical glitches made things worse. Meetings weren’t recorded automatically. The desktop app regularly got stuck. Adding tasks from my phone became a gamble because they wouldn’t reliably save. When you’re already juggling a lot of responsibilities, you need the tool to reduce overwhelm, not add to it. We’ve used Google Workspace for years, and we’re now looking at combining Gemini Apps & Gems with something like Trello or Jira. They’re easier to navigate, better supported, and more cost-effective. Motion has potential, but the gap between what it promises and what it currently delivers is too wide for me to justify the price or the learning curve.

I routinely find I am doing something dead simple that an agent will one-shot, e.g. add a new sort by option in the panel that lists a user's Linear tasks. If I looked at the PR diff I'd immediately think it was perfect and ship it. It's only when I actually get in there and play around with a dynamic UI that I realize, "you know this option really belongs at the top" or "hm, there's enough options here now that this dropdown feels cramped and we might need to consider another option". Simple examples obviously but the principle is that when I am landing the last 10% of a fix or a feature that when I need to interact and play-test. At the speed agents can generate fixes to new bugs or customer requests, I am bottle necked just doing that last 10% of steering and even the basic git mechanics to try something locally are enough to get me to not want to do it. Right now, it seems like the state of the art is to review PR diffs and just merge them in or if you are more sophisticated have your agent generate screenshots or screen recordings. Screenshots and images are moving in the right direction but if you are building something  interactive , you've really got to  interact  with it to know if it feels great. My dream was to start my day with an agent having handled every bug and small enhancement request that came my way that day, worked on, and ready for my review, so I could spend an hour each day just steering them to the finish line. I could do this linearly, picking off a branch an agent worked on, testing it and iterating but most of these small fixes each day aren't big brain stuff, I can effectively multi-task them but when I've tried doing it on my own machine it's either worktree hell, git gymnastics, or agents deadlocking - one agent wants to self test with Chrome MCP but can't cause another is editing code causing hot reloads. In Macro, any user can join the chat and steer the agent e.g. a colleague with UI taste jumps into tweak the last bits - I want to see common failure agentic failure cases across my team so I can improve our Claude.md and agentic practices so all work flowing through one interface allows that

If agents are good enough to reverse-engineer and workaround proprietary software today, the urgency to switch to open source decreases, not increases. "Good enough" workarounds are how SaaS stays sticky. And agents don't eliminate the trust problem, they move it. Today you trust Sunsama with your workflows. It's not "AI", but Motion's (not to be confused with Notion) algorithm is pretty good. When you add a task, you specify an urgency, time estimate, and what "schedule" it belongs to (e.g. work, personal, etc). Schedules are different categories with their own "slots" of time that a task can fill. You can also specify whether to use chunking, which lets the algorithm break a task into multiple events based on the "minimum chunk duration" you set for that task. For example, let's say you create a 9-5 "schedule" for work. It's currently 3pm. You add two tasks: - 3h, Task A, low priority, set min chunk duration to 1h - 1h, Task B, high priority Motion will schedule this as follows: - 3-4pm today, Task B - 4-5pm today, Task A - 9-11am tomorrow, Task A If you were to swap the urgencies, it will automatically reschedule those tasks (and any tasks that follow it, assuming they are marked as "auto-schedule") Tbh the only problem is it's price. The only issue that I ran into is one of the clients that I work for has a Microsoft Office suite that, unfortunately, I'm unable to connect my Outlook calendar to because you guys are not SOC 2 compliant, and I think you would also have to be HIPAA compliant in order for me to be able to connect that particular client.

Akiflow is my daily command center for current tasks.. Likes: It is the ideal program for creating a concrete weekly schedule. It is unrivaled in the "what we are doing today" panel and in quickly moving tasks, although for long-term strategic goals, I personally prefer a custom Notion template. The most important element, in my opinion, is the uniquely implemented **Timeslots**, which are the best I have seen. My entire weekly schedule is filled with them. They are set up cyclically, and when planning the next week over the weekend, I just fill them with tasks and make corrections if needed. This provides an excellent structure and saves a lot of time. The Timeslots allow me to easily shift entire blocks of work, serving as a template for my week. Akiflow's synchronization with Notion and automation capabilities are also great features. It automatically pulls tasks from various places in Notion to specific days, and its workflows then assign them to the appropriate timeslots. Akiflow, which I open hundreds of times a week via a shortcut, has given my life clear structure and was as much of a game-changer as Notion. It is faster and more efficient in day-to-day work. Dislikes: The speed of the Android app is lacking. It does not implement the management or planning of long-term goals, including subtasks.

Effortless Calendar Management with Minor Booking Issues. Likes: I use Reclaim.ai for managing my daily schedule, and it pulls across multiple calendars, both personal and work. I move tasks in, prioritize them, set deadlines, and Reclaim.ai ensures they are scheduled in time as prioritized activities that can't be easily overridden. I really like the ease of use and find the multiple calendar syncing very helpful. Having multiple separate calendars is useful for viewing on other apps and for sharing, and Reclaim.ai syncs these to avoid conflicts. Setting it up was easy. Dislikes: Reclaim.ai is not allowed to work with the NHS.net calendar, which is frustrating and could benefit from negotiation. The booking feature is limited on my plan and doesn't always work effectively, which can be a bit problematic.

A gentle nudge to focus when my day falls apart. Likes: Reclaim is one of a few tools I use to protect my focus in a world full of distractions. What I appreciate most is that it adapts when my calendar shifts around—and my calendar shifts a lot, even though I try to stick to a strict schedule. When my gym session or focus block gets bumped, Reclaim quietly reshuffles things and reminds me to actually focus. That nudge alone has been valuable. I also like the retrospective stats—looking back and seeing how much time I've genuinely spent focusing is satisfying, even though I know I'm not checking in on them as often as I should. It doesn't get every placement perfect (focus time sometimes lands in oddly random slots), but the trade-off for flexibility is worth it. Dislikes: Honestly, nothing stands out yet. I'm still an early user and I know I'm not using Reclaim to its full capacity, so I don't feel I've earned a strong critical opinion. If I become a power user, I might develop sharper views on what could be better. For now, it's doing what I need it to do—and I'm happy to keep using it.

Smart way to organize my schedule, scheduling meetings and my to-do list/tasks. Likes: Reclaim.ai is particularly valuable for protecting focus time in crowded calendars. Its ability to automatically prioritize and reschedule tasks and routines based on my real availability makes time management much more intentional and easier, without requiring constant manual adjustments on my end. It supports my time management efforts, shifting it from reactive to proactive. Instead of constantly negotiating calendar space, it helps me to create a system that enforces my priorities, creating some guardrails. Dislikes: Some advanced features are locked behind higher-tier plans, which can be a limitation depending on how deeply you want to integrate it into team workflows. Another limitation is that missed tasks or deadlines don’t always surface with strong alerts. It’s possible to overlook a task without it creating enough friction or escalation, which means I still need to be vigilant and, in some cases, duplicate reminders to avoid things slipping through.

Unified Calendar View with Helpful Conflict Notifications. Likes: I value the ability to consolidate calendars, have a controlled unified view of my schedule and received conflict notifications Dislikes: It needs a desktop app. 3-5 clicks to login via a browser is tardy.

Seamless Calendar Sync with Outstanding Support. Likes: I like the simple to use interface of Reclaim.ai, which makes it easy to navigate. The sync between my personal and work calendars is seamless, allowing me to manage both effortlessly. I appreciate the scheduling links that help streamline setting up meetings. The smart scheduling feature that works among multiple team members is great, especially since it can handle things automatically. I find it valuable that other team members can move meetings that don't work for them. There's also very impressive customer service and the initial setup was so easy. Dislikes: NA

Flexible Meeting Links and a Clear Daily Schedule Overview. Likes: I can create different kinds of links for meetings and special links for group meetings. I also love that Reclaim gives me a daily overview of my schedule. Dislikes: Haven't found anything I dislike about reclaim yet

Effortlessly Syncs Calendars and Tasks. Likes: I like the fact that Reclaim.ai works around my schedule, never touching the appointments that I already have, but creating buffers before and after them according to my specifications. I also like that it takes the tasks I enter and organizes them with the time left. There's also a feature similar to Calendly that adds stability for people to schedule time with me that closes the loop on organizing my time completely. Dislikes: The fact that reclaim always creates the tasks on the main calendar means that there's no way for me to look at my schedule without the reclaim changes. If I need to do something in the next two hours that was not on my schedule, reclaim would spend those entire 2 hours reshuffling my schedule and I will keep getting notified about it from my calendar. There needs to be a way to say "I stepped out", which will move tasks out of the way and stop refshuffling the calendar until I'm back. Some form of subtasks or a way to have a checklist in a task can be very useful. Tasks that take less than 15 min, which is more like a reminder to do something and check it off the list - that's just part of life, and we need that as well.

Effortless Scheduling with Intuitive Design. Likes: The thing I like most about Reclaim.ai is its ease of use and intuitive design, which just makes everything smoother. The smart booking for habits and tasks is fantastic because it means I don't have to think or worry about my bandwidth for the day ahead. My day is planned out by past me, so future me can just chill and follow the list of tasks in my calendar. The smart booking feature is great for scheduling things like competitive research and tasks you usually never make time for. It's awesome for setting priorities on different tasks I want to do. The biggest game changer for us has been the external calendar integration, which makes it easy for clients to book with our studio without the back-and-forth. Just sending them a link allows them to figure it out in their calendar, which I really appreciate. Also, the initial setup for Reclaim.ai is really easy, and its design is simple. Dislikes: It's a relatively new software service (as I understand), so the only thing I'm very eager to get working is API integration. That hasn't worked very well for us yet.

Great Weekly Task Overview That Makes Prioritizing Easy. Likes: It gives me an overall view of tasks I need to complete throughout the week and helps me prioritize which tasks I need to do first and which tasks can wait. Dislikes: I dislike that I cannot set a "task" to a certain time from the "create" page. You must create the task and then "lock" it in order for that task to not jump around the calendar.

Reclaim Keeps Multiple Calendars Perfectly Synced. Likes: I have multiple calendars that have to be kept synched: two businesses, clients, medical appointments, personal time. Reclaim is the only method I've found to keep everything from overlapping, and it works perfectly. It's worth every penny. Dislikes: There are a lot of settings; it's more sophisticated than intuitive.
